title: Will You Go, My Heart, with the One Who Has Gone?
intro: In a supplement to Mu'jiz Ahmad, Abd al-Majid Diyab prints this poem in praise of Ahmad ibn al-Hasan. A shorter version edited by Abd al-Aziz al-Maymani names Ja'far instead. In the fourteen verses heard here, al-Mutanabbi first talks to the heart that has deserted him. A cup of wine later brings him to his patron almost before the listener notices that the love poem has changed direction.

translation: Will you go, my heart, with the one who has gone?
I have lost two loves. Now I must mourn myself.
1.sharh: His heart is the second loved one to leave. He begins by addressing it as a travelling companion and ends by speaking as a mourner at his own funeral.

translation: How could I escape hurt, with the war of al-Basus
between my eyelids and sleep?
2.sharh: His sleeplessness feels like a feud between his eyelids and the first touch of sleep. The name of the long war between Bakr and Taghlib runs across the break in the middle of the verse.

translation: Am I still alive after you have gone,
when you, my heart, have left me, and my solace has gone?
3.sharh: He speaks first to those who have left, then singles out his heart. The other loss was the person in whom it found a home. Both departures sound almost the same in Arabic, binta and bana.

translation: May the full moon of night ransom that face,
and the sway of a bough that swaying walk.
4.sharh: A full moon for a face, a supple bough for a swaying figure. The moon and the bough usually set the standard of beauty. Here the lover would give them up to keep the face and the walk.

translation: What has parting to do with a company gathered together?
What have the winds to do with abandoned camps?
5.sharh: Parting scatters the people and the wind erases what their camp leaves behind. In each question two things meet that the lover wishes had never had anything to do with each other.

translation: As though he had never been, after being mine,
just as he was mine after he had not been.
6.sharh: He can scarcely believe the beloved was ever his. The two halves reverse the order of “was” and “was not”, going over the same words as someone might turn an astonishing piece of news over in his mind.

translation: As though he had never poured me wine
mixed with the moisture of his mouth in place of rainwater.
7.sharh: The “as though” carries over from the previous verse. What has become hard to believe is a moment of intimacy, when the moisture of the cupbearer's mouth took the place of the rainwater used to dilute wine.

translation: In his hand it has the colour of his cheeks
and your fragrance, Ahmad ibn al-Hasan.
8.sharh: The wine in the beloved's hand takes its red from his cheeks. The person addressed as “you” in the second half is Ahmad. The poet finds a way into his praise through the scent of the very same cup.

translation: Did the nobility of Ya'rub not find you
a marvel among the people of your time?
9.sharh: Arab nobility comes looking for someone to call its own and finds him a marvel of his age. The feminine noun for a rare or extraordinary thing lets the poet call a man a living wonder.

translation: As though the graces kept jealous watch over you
and drew the swords of strife in your presence.
10.sharh: The fine qualities become jealous guardians who draw swords around him. The language of a lover's jealousy follows the poem into praise, giving the rivalry over one man's gifts a scene of its own.

translation: The mention of you is sweeter than its fragrance,
and praise of you the sweetest sound the ear receives.
11.sharh: Saying Ahmad's name is a pleasure he can describe only in terms of scent. Praise then reaches its proper sense, hearing. The fragrance recalls the cup through which Ahmad first entered the poem.

translation: No one has set eyes on you
and still needed to ask, “Whose son is this?”
12.sharh: One look answers the question that would ordinarily establish a stranger's standing. The poet has gone to the trouble of naming Ahmad and his father, then tells us how little need there is to ask.

translation: If someone came asking even of a child of Tayy,
the child would share his milk with him.
13.sharh: A child too young to give money would still have something to give, his own milk. Al-Maymani reads the image as an extreme instance of generosity in Tayy, present even before a child can learn the custom.

translation: The only sea on land is your open hand.
In battle, Yemen alone has men.
14.sharh: A sea on dry land gives the measure of one man's generosity. In the second half, the poet extends the praise from the man to the Yemeni kindred of Tayy, reserving the name of men of valour for them.

1.1.1.head: ظَعَنَ
1.1.1.meaning: To leave one's encampment and travel on.

1.2.2.head: نَدَبَ
1.2.2.meaning: To lament the dead. He is already speaking of mourning himself.

2.1.5.head: البَسوس
2.1.5.meaning: Al-Basus, the long feud between Bakr and Taghlib. The final consonant of the name falls at the start of the next half.

2.2.5.meaning: Drowsiness, the first onset of sleep.

3.2.2.head: بانَ
3.2.2.meaning: You went away. He has turned back to address his heart.

3.2.5.meaning: Someone with whom one feels at rest, here the beloved.

4.1.1.head: فِدىً
4.1.1.meaning: A ransom, the price one would give to save another. The moon is the price offered here.

4.1.4-5.head: بَدر الدُّجى
4.1.4-5.meaning: “The full moon of darkness”, the bright moon seen against a dark night.

4.2.2.meaning: A swaying, supple movement. It can describe a walk or the bending of a bough.

5.1.4.head: الجَميع
5.1.4.meaning: A company gathered together, the people of the camp before their dispersal.

5.2.4.head: الدِّمَن
5.2.4.meaning: Traces of an encampment, such as hearth ash or marks left by animals after the people have moved on.

7.1.3.head: الرّاح
7.1.3.meaning: Wine, a frequent name for it in poetry.

7.2.1-2.head: ماء اللِّثى
7.2.1-2.meaning: “The water of the gums”, the moisture of the beloved's mouth.

7.2.5.head: المُزن
7.2.5.meaning: Rain clouds. Their water is the rainwater for mixing with wine. The reciter pronounces it muzan, with an a after the z.

8.2.3-5.head: أَحمَد بن الحَسَن
8.2.3-5.meaning: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, the patron named in this recording. Al-Maymani's version calls him Ja'far ibn al-Hasan in the verse.

9.1.2.head: أَلفى
9.1.2.meaning: To find or come upon. The subject of the verb is nobility itself.

9.1.4.head: اليَعرُبِيّ
9.1.4.meaning: Ya'rubi, named for Ya'rub, an ancestor in traditional accounts of the Arabs of Yemen.

9.2.2.head: غَريبَة
9.2.2.meaning: A rarity or marvel. The word is a feminine noun applied here to a man.

10.1.3-4.head: غارَ عَلى
10.1.3-4.meaning: To be jealously protective of someone. Here fine qualities themselves feel the jealousy.

10.2.1.head: سَلَّ
10.2.1.meaning: To draw a sword from its sheath.

11.1.4.head: نَشر
11.1.4.meaning: The fragrance given off by something sweet-smelling.

12.1.5.head: غَنِيَ
12.1.5.meaning: To have no need of something. The following half supplies what the onlookers can dispense with.

12.2.1.head: رُؤيا
12.2.1.meaning: The sight of someone while awake. The preceding “set eyes on” makes the sense clear.

13.1.5.head: طَيِّئ
13.1.5.meaning: Tayy, an Arab tribe traditionally traced to Yemen. Hatim, proverbial for hospitality, belonged to it.

13.2.2.head: قاصِد
13.2.2.meaning: A visitor who has come to ask for a gift, here from the child.

14.1.6.head: نَدى
14.1.6.meaning: Generosity or bounty. Al-Maymani's witness has “your two hands”, another way of speaking of giving.

14.2.4.head: البَأس
14.2.4.meaning: Might or valour in battle. The glottal stop is smoothed into a long vowel in the verse.

14.2.6.meaning: Yemen, standing for its people. The traditional descent of Tayy connects the final tribute to the patron.
